narrative:
The model estimated a 59.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is not a certainty, but it means the model judged failure more likely than success, and that risk was treated as too high for admission.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile in Year 3, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this was the strongest factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 24, compared with an accepted-student average of about 37, was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure. Between those, your lower-middle family-income bracket was the second most influential factor and actually pushed toward passing, reducing the estimated risk somewhat, though it was not enough to offset the academic indicators.

To strengthen a future application, focus on the areas most directly associated with the model’s concern: prepare to retake the LSAT with a structured course and practice tests, and address your upper-level academic record, especially the weak third-year standing, through additional coursework or a clear explanation of improvement. Meet with admissions advising to ask what evidence would demonstrate readiness, and consider delaying reapplication until you have stronger test scores and academic performance.
